2- The utilitarians themselves have split among themselves, and some among them have tried to temper the materialistic extremism in the view of human beings, their motives, and their actions.
For example, Stewart Mill (1776–1873) was one of the most ardent enthusiasts of his teacher Bentham, but he did not remain so for long. His enthusiasm waned, and he re-examined materialistic utilitarianism, revising it into intellectual utility. Whereas Bentham had preferred the utility of the individual over the utility of the community in case of conflict, Mill ultimately argued the opposite, insisting that the individual must sacrifice his happiness if it leads to the happiness of the community. He rejected the selfishness that Bentham had promoted and affirmed other-regardingness as the criterion for behavior. The individual's sacrifice of his own interests becomes obligatory for the good of others.
Thus, Mill rejects Bentham's evaluation of utility based on materialistic foundations, because he discovered that the sources of human behavior differ from those of animals, and therefore the basis of life differs between the two, and accordingly, the concept of animal pleasure differs from the concept of human pleasure. For human beings are unique in possessing reason, which inclines toward pleasures that are suitable for it. Few people are content in life with bestial pleasures that make them similar to beasts.
Here, human dignity, pride, modesty, and other such qualities are defined, which cannot originate from the same sources as those of animals. Often, human beings prefer poverty with freedom over wealth with servitude, and this is the central conflict we witness today on the world stage.

5. Utilitarianism

  1. Taking pleasure or utility as the sole criterion for moral behavior does not contribute to the progress of the individual or society. Both, whether the individual or the society, are driven forward by a higher ideal that they strive to achieve, and this ideal becomes the measure of their progress or regression.

Pleasure or utility cannot serve as such a higher ideal around which people unite, because pleasures, which are numerous, require a higher standard to distinguish between them. This is in the case of the individual. As for the community, pleasures conflict among its members, and utilities differ and contradict each other. Hence, it is impossible for pleasure or utility to be the best criterion for behavior. Islamic morality differs from other kinds of secular morality in that it presents itself as practical ethics that do not admit of debate. Rules every translator (human or model) follows, so a book translated in pieces reads as one voice.

Principles

  • Faithful, complete, readable. Translate every heading, paragraph, quotation and footnote. Do not summarise, skip, soften,
    sharpen or comment. The author's argument and tone are his; the translation does not endorse or correct them.
  • Natural scholarly English, not word-for-word. Keep the author's sentence rhythm where it can be done without strain.
  • The text is OCR from a scan. Silently repair obvious OCR slips (missing hamza, a swapped letter, a split word) when the
    meaning is clear from context. If a passage is truly unreadable, write [illegible] and keep going. Never invent text.
  • Keep the Markdown structure: #/##/### headings, paragraphs, lists, --- rules and <sup> as in the source.
  • Footnotes: the source marks them (١), (٢)…; write (1), (2)… and keep each footnote text. Translate titles of cited

Second: Trust (Tawakkul)

Its Relation to the Oneness of God (Tawhid):

Trust is the fruit of the oneness of God, and a criterion for the Muslim's belief in divine decree and predestination. It is evidence of the individual's understanding and correct perception of his power and the limits of his power. Thus, he does not become deluded or excessive in relying solely on his own strength and ability as the only cause for achieving his goals. Rather, his heart is confident in God Almighty, as the cause of causes and the guide to the path of good and success. He entrusts his affairs to his Creator, who controls all of his matters, from life to sustenance, because:

"And no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in which land it will die." (55)

The Meaning of Trust:

Trust means that a person exerts effort within the limits and commands of the Sharia, and then leaves the results of his effort to God Almighty.

Its Effect:

This balanced and tranquil stance fills the individual's heart and soul with peace, safety, and contentment. Thus, in the case of success, his state is one of determination and noble perseverance, unaware of failure or despair. When the results he hoped for through his effort do not materialize, he becomes more determined and resolute in rationalizing his means and reassessing his position. In this lies the development of his abilities and capacities, and the improvement of his tools and methods. These are the causes of progress and success in achieving good and happiness, whether for the individual or for nations.

If, however, his effort results in achieving what he hoped for, he does not become arrogant or conceited, for these are causes of tyranny and stagnation. Rather, he becomes grateful for the favor of God and His blessings, and he calls upon success to increase his humility, which in turn increases his ambition to attain perfection and progress.

Third: Intention

Intention, desire, and will are all one in meaning.
Its meaning is the direction of the heart toward choosing one matter over another with a firm resolve, between which there is no obstacle except something external to the will.
In Islam, intention is the standard for determining the value of an action and judging it as good or evil, because if the intention of the doer with his action is for the face of God, the action is good, and its doer deserves praise and reward. And if the intention is for something other than God, the action is judged according to the intention behind it, whether it is for a good or bad reason. If it is for evil, the intention is evil, and its doer is wicked and deserves censure and punishment. But if it is for something permissible, it is an ordinary action that does not deserve evaluation by the standard of good or evil.
Thus, the action takes the ruling of the intention in it, hence it was said: "Indeed, deeds are but by intentions."
So, it is without intention, it has no ruling in itself in terms of good or evil; rather, it is the intention that God bestows upon it one of the two descriptions and determines its moral nature.
Therefore, in this regard, intentional behavior in Islam is divided into three categories:

First: Acts of Worship

These are connected to intention in the basis of their validity, because intention is a condition for the validity of performing religious duties, which are not complete except when the Muslim intends the face of God with them and they are exclusive to Him alone and to none else. This is the rank of sincerity and the peak of moral perfection in Islam.
For example, giving money to the poor is, in itself, good in the eyes of the poor and according to the religious law that commanded it. These are all matters in which there is neither a command nor a prohibition from the Shari'a. However, if an intention is present, it takes the ruling of that intention. So, when a Muslim performs such an act with the intention of good, seeking the face of God, it becomes a moral act and an obedience for which the doer is rewarded.

The mixing of motives:
This is the matter of intention as a criterion for determining the nature and description of an action.
So, theoretically, it is clear and easy to divide behavior into obedience, disobedience, and permissibility. But reality is more complex and intertwined. We cannot precisely determine the original motive behind our actions, nor can we be certain that a single motive is sufficient to drive us to perform an action. In other words, it is difficult for someone who extends a hand to help a needy person to clearly identify whether the motive behind the action is personal, human, religious, or all of them together.
This is an issue that determines the presence in our hearts of moral goodness or hypocrisy and pretense.

Imam Ghazali dealt with this issue with great precision, and he tried to establish a criterion by which an individual could choose his motive and intention to determine its true direction. He argues that when a person's will is torn between the motive of morality and the motive of self-interest, and the matter becomes confused for him in determining which is the primary driving force behind his action, he must test the effect of each motive separately, as if it were the sole motive behind the action, and then analyze its relationship with the other motive. This relationship does not fall outside of three conditions:

  • Companionship (al-muraqabah): This means that two motives are present, each of which is sufficient on its own to complete the action.
  • Participation (al-musharaka): This means that two motives are present, neither of which is sufficient on its own to complete the action, but the action is completed through their joint presence.
  • Assistance (al-mua'ana): This means that one of the motives is sufficient on its own to complete the action, while the other merely facilitates its performance.

These are the three scenarios of the coexistence of motives, and the individual must measure the strength of his moral motive in relation to the other motive.

If the two scales are equal, that is, the moral motive and the personal motive in performing the action are balanced, the action is neutral and cannot be described as moral or immoral.

However, if the scale of the moral motive outweighs the other motives, the action possesses a degree of moral value corresponding to the strength and dominance of the moral motive over the other.

Conversely, if the scale of the personal motive outweighs the moral motive, the action loses its moral value.

These scenarios are clarified by the following example:

Suppose someone asks you for help, and let us assume that he is entitled to it for two reasons: poverty and kinship. You then provide him with the help he requested.

So that you may know the moral value of your action, and whether it was done with the intention of benefiting the other,

If you find in yourself the same determination and joy in helping both, then this is evidence that your relation to the motive is equal.
Each of the two motives—i.e., the motive of kinship and the motive of poverty—has an equal power over you as the power of the other motive. And this is the case of companionship in motives.

But if the rich relative or the poor foreigner do not benefit from your goodness, then this is evidence that neither of the two motives, individually, is sufficient to move your will to act. And this is the case of participation.

And if you find that the original motive is poverty and need, and the other motive is merely a facilitator and a helper, without being able to move your soul or stir your spirit on its own,
then this is evidence that the first motive is superior and holds dominance, while the other is secondary and its absence does not prevent the action from being completed. And this is the case of assistance.

Therefore, if the two motives are equal, i.e., the religious and the personal, or the obligatory and the beneficial, the moral charge in the action is nullified due to the balance of the positive and negative in it.

But if the moral motive prevails, then it has a moral advantage over the other motive in proportion to its strength.

Likewise, in the opposite case, the action is ugly to the extent of the difference in strength between the two motives, but it does not reach the ugliness of an action devoid of any moral motive, because even the slightest inclination in our will toward good creates an equal amount of good and light in our souls, and this in itself is evidence of the superiority of Islamic morality over other human morals.

Moderation and Balance:

But a significant question arises here: If the character of Islamic ethics is balance or moderation between excess and deficiency, how can we in reality determine this balance or moderation in relation to each of our obligations?

Can reason determine this middle path?

Or is it the individual conscience entrusted with this application?

This question directly brings us to the core of the moral problem, which philosophers, ancient and modern, have addressed with different solutions, and which the theologians in Islamic thought have posed in this way: What is the standard of obligation? The Sharia or reason?

The Ash'arites held that the Sharia is the basis of moral responsibility, while reason has no weight in this path.

The Mu'tazilites, on the contrary, made reason the basis, while the Sharia confirms what reason has established.

It is clear that both approaches suffer from excess or deficiency, for reason cannot do without the Sharia in moral legislation, and the legislator cannot do without reason in responsibility and implementation.

133: Take, for example, the way a person performs his worship of his Creator. If each individual were left to organize this worship as he pleases, the matter would not be free of one of two possibilities: Either he would remain confused and do nothing, or he would resort to all sorts of imagination and arbitrariness. This is evident in the extremes of some ascetics and others who rely on their personal efforts to determine how to perform their duties, and they end up in neglect or in reprehensible excess. And in other human fields, the truth remains consistent. For instance, what are our duties toward our emotional nature and our physical desires? Should we be virtuous people by suppressing them and not responding to them, and imposing all sorts of harshness upon ourselves, as the Manichaeans did? Or is it sufficient to pretend indifference to all kinds of good and evil in the world, and to resort to complete silence and inactivity, as the Stoics did? Or should we seek happiness by indulging in sensory pleasures and enjoying them as much as we can, as the Sophists, Cyrenaics, and Utilitarians did? All these schools of thought, as we saw in the previous chapters, were based on a self-centered tendency, which urges the adherent to act in accordance with that tendency as he perceives it to the best of his ability. The same is true in what concerns our relations with others, for finding the appropriate behavior is no less difficult due to the differing views on the nature of such relationships. For example, should a person who has been insulted by another seek retaliation or forgive, or does he have a choice between retaliation and forgiveness?

Second: Conditions for its Performance

The material ability to perform the act, and its falling under individual capability:

The Islamic obligation is not an obligation that is fulfilled through: arbitrariness or inimitability regarding hardship. Rather, it is an obligation that requires rising to meet it within the limits of human ability. What else could it be? Not like an obligation (« was ) which does not take into account the condition of the one performing it, thus remaining an empty matter, flying far away from human ability.

The Qur'an has established this condition in its statement: "Allah does not burden a soul except [with that within] its capacity," (2:286).

Here, ability encompasses the condition of the doer, and also the condition of the non-doer.

The condition of the doer is in terms of the act entering under his knowledge, his will, and his ability.

This becomes clear from the statement of the Messenger ﷺ:

"Three things were lifted from my nation: error, forgetfulness, and what they are compelled to do." (104)

"Three things are excused: the sleeper until he awakens, the insane until he recovers, and the child until he grows up." (105)

The Qur'an is explicit in stating and defining the type of knowledge that serves as the basis for moral responsibility, and it is clear that human capacities are suitable for legislation and moral responsibility, in its statement: "And we would not have punished until we sent a messenger." (106)

As for the condition of the act: the acts that do not fall under the will or ability of the doer, such as the whispering of the self and fleeting thoughts, and what is woven in the self from inclinations and natural desires, and natural acts, are not subject to obligation.

The Ease in Performance

Islamic ethics do not merely exclude what is absolutely impossible or beyond individual capacity, but they also reject any obligation that is not usually bearable. Islam reaches the point of ease by observing the absence of hardship and excessive effort, even if it is within the capacity of the performer.

This is because the message that Islam insists on conveying to those who are obligated is: "Allah intends for you ease, and not hardship (107)." And "He has not placed upon you in religion any difficulty (108)." And "It is not for Allah to lighten for you (109)."

This ease is practically evident in the concessions that Islam has provided to ease the burden on its followers in fulfilling its obligations, such as shortening prayers during travel, fasting for nursing and pregnant women when there is a fear of harm, and other similar concessions.

The general principle upon which Islam builds its moral foundation is what the Messenger ﷺ declared: "No harm and no reciprocating harm," based on what the Qur'an explicitly stated, that obligations must be executed in ordinary circumstances. However, in cases of emergency, the obligation is nullified.

Any command or prohibition is waived automatically when harm results from its performance or when it becomes impossible to carry it out. This is clear from the statement of Allah:

Thus, we are before a precise and refined system that radiates mercy and perfection, considered a unique legislation in the realm of ethics.
While ethical doctrines place moral rules as commands independent of time, place, the condition of the doer, and the feasibility of the action,
we find Islam introducing a new element in moral obligation: taking into account the condition of the doer, the feasibility and ease of performing the action, and avoiding hardship.
At the same time, the field for ascending to the peaks of human perfection remains open before those who are determined.
Both conditions—the condition of the doer and the feasibility of the action—merge the meaning of divine wisdom and justice on one hand, and the mercy and compassion that distinguish the exalted Divine Being on the other. Third: Rights and Duties

We would first like to emphasize some matters that we find essential to understanding the meaning of rights and duties in Islam.

First: The study of rights and duties arises from the need of human beings for happiness, and happiness is a feeling based on satisfaction, security, and tranquility, which is available only to the soul that feels the goodness of itself and the life it lives in. This feeling is available only to the person who believes in the correctness of his belief and his goodness, and that he is under the guarantee of an all-powerful, perfect, creating, and capable, just and merciful Being, who alone is able to determine his rights and duties, which ensure for him security and happiness in this world and the hereafter, and to reward the good-doer and punish the wrongdoer, not only in this world but also in another eternal and lasting life.

Thus, rights and duties depend more on revelation than on reason, and this is what the Qur'an expressed in its statement: > "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with injustice, those are the ones who have security, and they are the ones who are rightly guided." (Al-An'am 6:82) So whoever follows My guidance will not go astray nor will he grieve, but whoever turns away from My remembrance, then indeed, he will have a difficult life." (Ta-Ha 20:123-124)

Second: In Islam, rights and duties are based on a balance in satisfying the physical and spiritual aspects equally, and it does not welcome those who are consumed by one duty or right at the expense of their other duties and rights. The Messenger ﷺ said to one who wanted to devote himself entirely to worship: > "Fast and break your fast, stand in prayer and sleep, for your body has a right upon you, your eyes have a right upon you, your wife has a right upon you, and your guest has a right upon you." Third: Rights and Duties in Islam Rest on Two Pillars:

The First: Sincerity, meaning that the motivation for fulfilling a duty and attaining a right must be love of God and obedience to Him. The Messenger explained this, saying:

"None of you believes until Allah and His Messenger are more beloved to him than anything else." (122)

The Second Pillar: Ability, meaning the personal capacity to perform the task. When He says: "So stand firm as you have been commanded," (123) the condition for undertaking the task is ability. It does not please Him that our breaths be cut short in the pursuit of duty, until we despair of ever catching up with it. We are only encouraged to perform it and to continue in it when the hardship and burden are removed from it. He says, exalted be He:

"Allah does not burden a soul except with what it can bear." (124); "Allah intends ease for you, and the affairs of humanity will be difficult except for those whom He has favored—those who walk in moderation." (125); "except for those who are forced, while their hearts are at rest with faith." (126) Thus, the essence of command is mercy and compassion, and this is the content of the message in His saying:

"And We did not send you except as a mercy to the worlds." (127)

Fourth: Rights and Duties in Islam are Ethical in the Full Sense

As we have already established in our discussion of types of responsibility, all of them become ethical responsibilities when we commit internally to fulfilling them. From this perspective, all duties and rights commanded by the Shari'a become ethical duties and rights in relation to the Muslim, because Islam, as we have often stated, in its true meaning, is complete submission and perpetual obedience—intellectually, emotionally, and physically—to Allah the Exalted.

Fifth: The reciprocity between rights and duties is based on equivalence. The human being has multiple relationships, the most important of which are: his relationship with God, his relationship with himself and with others, and his relationship with the natural world.

As for his relationship with God: it is a relationship between the lower and the higher, and there can be no reciprocity between right and duty in it. Rather, the higher, which is God, has an absolute right in the obedience of the lower, and the lower, which is the human being, has an absolute duty in the worship of God through obedience and devotion. For the meaning of the human having a right over God is that God is bound to fulfill this right, and binding implies a limitation of God’s will and choice. This would contradict the absolute perfection of God. Absolute perfection means absolute will and choice.

The Noble Qur’an decisively clarifies this relationship between God and His creation in its statement: “To Him belongs all that is in the heavens and the earth. He does not take anyone as a partner, and He will not be questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.” (21:23) (129). “And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.” (51:56) (130). This is from one perspective.

From another perspective, the absolute right of God in the obedience of His servant is what gives legitimacy and morality to the rights that the human being enjoys in his relationship with himself and with others. For the duty of obedience and servitude is the foundational legal and moral basis for all the duties that a person undertakes in his relationship with himself and with others.

As for the relationship of the individual with himself and with others: the principle in it is equivalence and equality. And from this arises the reciprocity between rights and duties. Every right is matched by a duty, and every duty is matched by a right. Islam has clarified this relationship based on equivalence and equality in its statement: “O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul and created from it his wife and dispersed from the two of them many men and women.” (49:13) (131). “O mankind, indeed We created you from a male and a female and made you into nations and tribes that you may know one another.” (49:13) (132).

Rights and Duties

The basis of the correlation between rights and duties is justice and equality.
Rights and duties form a chain. There is a duty to God that does not correspond to a right of man,
and there is a right of man in nature that does not correspond to a duty of nature itself.

Sixthly: Many moral philosophers argue that rights and duties are social phenomena, meaning that they cannot be conceived to exist except in a community. Thus, if a person were to live in an isolated desert, the meaning of right and duty would not be conceivable.

However, in light of what we have established previously, it becomes clear that this view is incorrect. For the responsibility of the individual, or his rights and duties, is based on revelation. This is from one perspective.
From another perspective, since the human soul is a complex and composite fabric of diverse powers, full of various motives and inclinations that compete with one another, each pushing the person to fulfill its desire without restriction or condition,
if the matter were left without a standard or criterion to determine the duties and rights of each power, the balance between the powers of the soul would be disrupted, and it would incline toward excess or deficiency, causing the structure of personality to collapse and tear in every direction. The task of true ethics is to establish an appropriate method to satisfy the different aspects of personality in a way that achieves its security and stability.

Indeed, the scope of rights and duties may narrow, but they do not disappear, for the human being, as we said, has a relationship with his Lord, a relationship with himself, and a relationship with society, and these relationships are regulated by revelation. If his relationship with society ends, the rights and duties that regulate his other relationships remain.

Thus, rights and duties are inseparable from the human being as long as he remains a rational and volitional human being, whether as an individual or in a community.
145:
Meaning of Right and Duty

Right is what you are entitled to enjoy, act upon, and defend within the limits of divine command. Your life is a blessing granted to you by God, and no one has the right to encroach upon it with falsehood or to stand in the way of its growth and prosperity.

As for duty, it is everything the Shari'a commands you to do, whether by action or omission. Examples include prayer, fasting, zakat, pilgrimage, preserving your life, religion, and honor, fulfilling covenants and trust, honoring parents, defending yourself, your honor, property, and homeland, performing work with excellence, prohibiting unjust killing, adultery, theft, drinking alcohol, gambling, lying, cheating, hypocrisy, backbiting, betrayal, arrogance, and consuming people's wealth through falsehood, speaking falsely, and acting upon falsehood. All these are duties upon you to adhere to and to exert all your strength to fulfill them in the most complete manner.

The relationship between right and duty:

Right and duty are two sides of the same coin. Every right corresponds to a duty, and vice versa. If it is your right to look in every direction, it is your duty to avert your gaze from what is forbidden and from people's secrets. If it is your right that others do not threaten your life, it is your duty to direct that life toward what benefits them rather than harms them.

Every duty entails a right, and every right entails a duty. The relationship between right and duty is like the relationship between authority and responsibility. The more authority, the more responsibility; the more responsibility, the more authority. Authority without responsibility means oppression and stagnation, while responsibility without authority means weakness and inaction. If duty is the responsibility we must fulfill, then our right is the strength that enables us to shoulder the burdens of the duties we are entrusted with. From this, it is easy to understand our rights when we understand our duties. The duty of the father is nothing but the right of the child, and the duty of the child is nothing but the right of the father. Thus, in every right and duty.

147:
Duties

We will examine them from several considerations: in terms of performance, in terms of function, in terms of obligation, and in terms of relationship.

First: In terms of performance:

By performance of duty, one means that the individual's motivation in fulfilling his duties is God, in the sense that his will in performing these duties coincides with the will of the Sharia and its objectives.

Performing the duty in the correct manner requires that it be purely for the sake of God. It should not be tainted with elements of show, hypocrisy, ostentation, or the various desires of the self. A person must perform the duty because it is an obligation imposed upon him by his religion, not in expectation of benefit or fear of punishment. Those who perform their duties while their hearts are attached to the benefit or punishment involved are slaves to their own selves and their desires. In contrast, the free individuals with strong wills and pure consciences are those who perform what they are committed to in terms of duties, even if it contradicts their personal interests. They are the ones who raise the voice of God above the voice of their own selves. Through them, truth prevails, virtue dominates, goodness and happiness spread, and on their shoulders alone does the edifice of human civilization stand on solid foundations of truth, justice, and peace. No nation has ever been lost except when the voice of desire overpowers the voice of duty in the consciences of its individuals.

Dr. Muhammad Abdullah Draz says: "The goal that the pious believer should aim for in his activity while performing his duty does not lie in the good things of this world, nor in joy and glory in the hereafter, nor in satisfying his sense of goodness, nor in completing his inner existence. It is God, God, who should be before our eyes." (136)

148:
Second: In Terms of Function

The obligatory duties are divided in this regard into:

(a) Positive duties, which are the obligations and religious commands that require us to perform actions.

(b) Negative duties, which are the commands that prohibit us from performing actions.

Positive duties indicate to us what we must do towards our Creator, towards ourselves, and towards others, so that we may attain goodness and happiness.

(b) As for negative duties, they indicate to us what we must not do. They represent the fundamental conditions that must be present for positive duties to bear fruit. Their function is to remove obstacles and create a suitable environment for the growth and flourishing of positive duties.

Thus, the prohibition of killing is the fundamental condition for the survival and reproduction of the human species; the prohibition of adultery is the fundamental condition for the security and stability of life; and the prohibition of theft is a condition for the economic and social prosperity of society.

Therefore, prohibitions represent the necessary conditions for the individual and society to fulfill their functions, by providing security and stability. As for the commands, they are the conditions for their prosperity and attainment of perfection.

Third: As for the obligation:

It is divided into:

(a) Fundamental and essential duties. These are specific and must be carried out without exception. Islam does not accept any compromise or delay in them. They include all the prohibited acts, such as killing, sedition, banditry, adultery, theft, rape, usury, drinking alcohol, lying, backbiting, envy, deceit, hypocrisy, and other major sins. They also include the duties that are incumbent on every individual, such as prayer, fasting, zakat, pilgrimage, honoring parents, fulfilling covenants, honesty, trustworthiness, enjoining good, and forbidding evil, among other duties.
149:
This section, which includes negative and positive duties, represents the minimum of Islamic ethics that protects the individual and the community from falling below what virtue and happiness require. It is the essential limit for human safety and happiness. Therefore, we find the Shariah encourages the performance of these duties through rewards and punishments.

(b) Duties such as those the Shariah calls mustahabb (recommended), which are not fixed in quantity, except for excess, and are not obligatory in execution. In this regard, it says: "Let those who contend contend." (137) This opens up avenues for advancement for those with literary aspirations who: "Prefer themselves even though hardship might be upon them." (1308) And those who race in good deeds and respond with what is best.

"And He feeds the hungry, the orphan, and the poor, with love." (139)

Performing these duties is what fosters bonds of love, mercy, affection, unity, mutual compassion, empathy, cooperation, and all the virtues that drive the individual and society toward high realms of good and happiness.

But since these duties are not within the reach of every will, they are optional, not compulsory, and there is no punishment for neglecting them; rather, the Shariah encourages them through reward alone.

Fourth: As for the relationship:

We said that man has multiple relationships: a relationship with his Creator, a relationship with himself, and a relationship with others. Islam has organized and perfected these relationships through a set of duties. And there is no one who wants to preserve his guidance (138) who would neglect them.

First: The Individual's Duties Toward His Material Being

By this we mean taking care of one's body and physical health, for the body is the vehicle that carries the individual toward his goals. The stronger a person's physical condition, the greater his hope of achieving his objectives and fulfilling his moral responsibilities.

For this reason, taking care of physical health is among the foremost moral duties. Virtues such as generosity, courage, patience, and perseverance in work require a healthy body. It was said long ago, "A sound mind is in a sound body," and it is sufficient to confirm the validity of this relationship by observing the effects of poor digestion, for example, and diseases of the respiratory system, intestinal disorders, and other physical ailments on a person's mood, behavior, and outlook on life.

While we find that physical health often leads to optimism, high aspirations, self-confidence, and the ability to endure hardships and persevere in work, we also find that a weakened body leads to pessimism, depression, anxiety, and an inability to continue working. It spoils for the person the pleasures of life that are permitted, and it begets many moral and psychological vices, such as suspicions, hatred, and selfishness, because his thoughts often revolve around a single subject: his health problem and his inability to keep up with the healthy, who are helped by their physical health to achieve their hopes and dreams and fulfill their duties, and who possess confidence and optimism.

For this reason, Islam has shown the utmost concern for the duties that lead to preserving a person in his body and promoting its growth and strength. The strong believer is better and more beloved to God than the weak believer. Among the most important duties that a Muslim must observe are:

Cleanliness

The Muslim must take care of the cleanliness of his body, clothing, home, place of prayer, and public places. Islam is built upon cleanliness, and it is the religion of cleanliness, which made purity an obligation and an act of worship, and a cause of God's love and pleasure.

By this is meant preserving one's consciousness, mind, and will.

The feelings such as love and hatred, joy and sorrow, safety and fear, inclination and aversion, and other emotions are prior in existence in man than the mind and the will. It is the vessel of the sharara, and it accompanies the individual from his cradle to his grave. Indeed, it is among the most sensitive and most receptive of the spiritual aspects in man to stimulation and influence. Thus, when a person loves something, he surrenders himself to it and finds everything easy in its way. Conversely, if he hates something, he turns away from it and shuns any effort in its direction. Therefore, the future of man in happiness or misery depends largely on how his emotions are directed and on the subject that captures his love and attention. For example, if a person is obsessed with wealth, and the accumulation of wealth is the primary subject of his emotions and consciousness, then he will dedicate his activities and values to serving this purpose. At that point, he becomes a social and moral problem, no less dangerous than a thief who does not know evil or wickedness. The lover of wealth does not care what means he adopts to achieve his goal, whether lawful or unlawful, good or evil, right or wrong. What matters to him is the accumulation of wealth. Thus, it becomes the end that justifies all means for him. Indeed, he may resort to deception, fraud, lying, betrayal, and sell his honor for the sake of his beloved. This may lead him to the loss of every moral sense, so that he convinces himself that whatever achieves his purpose is lawful and right. This is the morality of the age, which has reached such a level of distortion that it justifies and even approves of wickedness.

Moreover, we cannot, no matter how much effort and time we exert, present the details of Islamic practical ethics, for it is as vast as life itself, in space and time. If he finds himself possessing all the virtues in it, then that is a sign of good character. If he lacks all of them, then that is a sign of bad character. Allah, the Exalted, said:

"Indeed, the successful are the believers. Those who are humble in their prayer, and who turn away from [idle] talk, and who are performers of zakat, and who guard their private parts, except from their wives or [lawful] what their right hands possess, for indeed, they are not to be blamed. But whoever seeks beyond that, then those are the transgressors. And those who are guardians of their trusts and their covenants. And those who are steadfast in their prayers. Those are the inheritors. They will inherit Paradise and dwell therein forever." (The Believers 21:1–1)

"(Those who are) the ones who remember Allah, standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth and say, 'Our Lord, indeed You did not create this in vain, exalted be You. So protect us from the punishment of the Fire." (The Believers 21:1)

"(Indeed, the believers are) those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, it increases them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely. Those who establish prayer and from what We have provided them, they spend." (Repentance 9:1)

They spend. Those are the true believers; for them are degrees with their Lord, forgiveness, and a noble provision (216).
(And the servants of the Most Merciful, who walk upon the earth humbly, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace." And those who spend the night in worship of their Lord, prostrating themselves and standing. And those who say, "Our Lord, remove from us the punishment of Hell. Indeed, its punishment is grievous. Indeed, it is an evil place of rest and an evil place to dwell." And those who, when they spend, do not squander wastefully nor do they stint, but are balanced between those extremes. And those who do not invoke with God another deity, nor kill a soul which God has forbidden to be killed except for the right reason, nor commit fornication. And whoever does this will encounter a sin. For him, the punishment will be multiplied on the Day of Resurrection, and he will dwell in it in disgrace. Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds; for those, God will transform their evil deeds into good deeds, and indeed, God is Forgiving, Merciful. And whoever repents and does good deeds, indeed, he will return to God in repentance. And those who do not bear witness to falsehood, and when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity. And those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord, do not fall deaf and blind to them. And those who say, "Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and offspring comfort to our eyes, and make us leaders for the pious." Those will be rewarded with Paradise for what they endured, and they will receive in it greeting and peace. Dwelling in it forever, a good place of rest and a good place to dwell (217).
